units.title: Two diaries: a book cart and a rehearsal
units.alignmentNote: Two separately complete original diary tasks, each four gaps and five sentences with one unused option, paired as a practice. The source supplies the single-diary task rules, not copied text or independent workload calibration.

materials.title: A. The travelling book cart
materials.text:
Friday, 12 June

Yesterday our class took a small book cart to the junior school. Each of us chose two books that younger children might enjoy. ____1____ I had read both stories myself, so I hoped I could answer questions about them.

At first, we arranged all the books by size. The table looked neat, but the children kept asking which stories had animals or adventures. ____2____ Soon they could find the subjects they wanted without opening every book.

A boy selected my book about a fox, then put it back. I asked what was wrong. He liked the pictures, but some words were difficult. ____3____ After a few pages, he began reading short lines aloud with me.

Before leaving, we wrote down which books had attracted the most interest. I had expected the thickest books to be the most popular. In fact, one thin picture book had a line of children waiting for it. ____4____ Next time, I will pay more attention to what readers ask for than to how large a book looks.
candidates: A. We made simple subject signs and moved the books into groups.
B. That surprised me and changed my idea of a useful choice.
C. I chose a fox story and a book about a journey by train.
D. So we stopped the visit and locked every book away.
E. I offered to read the first part with him.
materials.instruction: Read the complete diary. Choose one sentence for each gap. Use each option at most once; one sentence is not needed.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: C names the two selected books, which both stories in the next sentence refers to. A concerns later grouping, B a later surprise and E shared reading; D contradicts the continuing successful visit.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: A answers children asking for subjects and leads to finding them without checking each book. C only lists the narrator's books, B needs a surprising result, E a particular struggling reader; D would stop access.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: E responds to difficult words and leads directly to reading together. A is classification, B surprise and C initial choices. D closes rather than supports the visit.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: B reacts to the unexpected popularity of a thin book and prepares the changed selection principle. A and C belong earlier, E concerns one reader, and D contradicts recording a successful visit.

materials.title: B. A rehearsal in the courtyard
materials.text:
Sunday, 7 September

Yesterday we rehearsed a short play in our school courtyard. Our classroom stage was being repaired, so the teacher found another place for us to practise. ____1____ We could move freely, but at first it was difficult to imagine where the audience would sit.

We used empty chairs to mark the front row. Then our teacher stood behind them and asked us to repeat the opening scene. ____2____ She could hear the words, but a tree hid one actor whenever he stepped to the left.

We changed the position of the pretend doorway and tried again. This time all the actors remained in view. A friend watched from the far end and checked whether the small objects in our hands were clear. ____3____ We chose a larger one so that its role in the story would be easier to recognise.

Near the end, a group of younger students stopped to watch. We invited them to sit in the chairs. Their laughter helped us see which moments they understood. ____4____ It did not replace a rehearsal on the real stage, but it taught us to think about the view from the seats as well as the view from our own side.
candidates: A. A tiny letter looked like an empty hand from that distance.
B. The courtyard gave us more space than our usual room.
C. We decided that nobody would ever be allowed to watch the play.
D. The unexpected audience made the practice more useful.
E. From that position, she noticed a problem we had missed.
materials.instruction: Read the complete diary. Choose one sentence for each gap. Use each option at most once; one sentence is not needed.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: B develops the alternative courtyard space and links to moving freely. A concerns prop visibility, D the later audience and E the teacher's viewpoint. C contradicts eventually inviting watchers.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: E refers to standing behind the front row and introduces the tree blocking an actor. A concerns a later prop, B space and D the eventual audience. C conflicts with the rehearsal's purpose.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: A identifies a small letter as the unclear object, giving larger one in the next sentence a clear referent. B, D and E do not name the object, while C contradicts seeking audience understanding.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: D summarises the younger spectators' useful laughter. B is initial space, E the earlier visibility check and A the prop; C contradicts inviting them to sit.

units.title: Two guides: equipment and an audio programme
units.alignmentNote: Pairs two complete original five-gap/seven-option guides. Each preserves three printed headings, a quoted reminder at gap2 and a missing heading at gap5 as in the recorded specific task. No additional use-once rule is imposed; two options are unused in each guide.

materials.title: A. Sharing equipment for a group activity
materials.text:
A class activity may require stopwatches, clipboards and other shared equipment. Before collecting it, ask each group what they actually need. Some may need several clipboards but no stopwatch. ____1____ Taking equal quantities without discussing the tasks can leave useful items sitting unused.

Agree on a borrowing rule

Keep the arrangement simple enough for everyone to remember. At the start, a group member can say, "____2____" This makes it easier to find out where something has gone without accusing anyone of taking it secretly.

Make similar items recognisable

Several identical boxes can easily be confused when groups work nearby. ____3____ A clear label is more useful than expecting everyone to remember which box was originally beside which chair.

Check before returning

Do not simply place a closed box on the shelf. Check its contents against the list that came with it. ____4____ If a stopwatch has stopped working, explain that too rather than leaving the next user to discover it.

____5____

After the activity, ask whether any items were difficult to obtain or rarely used. Keep a short note for the next organiser. The aim is to make the next collection fit the actual tasks, not to borrow the greatest possible number of objects.
candidates: A. Attach the group name to the outside of each box.
B. We will tell one another before moving equipment to another group.
C. Learn from the equipment use
D. Discuss those different needs before deciding the quantities.
E. This helps ensure that the next group receives a complete set.
F. A closed lid proves that nothing can be missing.
G. Borrow every item first and ask about its purpose afterwards.
materials.instruction: Read the complete guide. Choose the best option for each gap. Two options are not needed. Keep the printed headings and quotation marks.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: D develops different task needs and leads to the warning against equal quantities. A is labelling, B a borrowing reminder, C the final heading and E complete returns. F and G encourage assumptions the guide rejects.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: B is a first-person quoted reminder to communicate movement, explaining how to locate items. A is an external labelling instruction, C a heading, D planning and E a result of checking. F and G undermine accountability.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: A supplies the visible label mentioned next. B is the quoted rule, C final review, D quantity planning and E the return check. F concerns an unjustified closed-lid assumption and G premature borrowing.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: E explains checking contents against the list and prepares reporting faults. A, B and D concern earlier stages, C is a heading. F contradicts checking and G ignores need.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 5.
questions.explanation: C is the heading for reflection on actual equipment use. A, B, D and E are sentences for earlier tasks rather than this heading; F and G contradict the reflective approach.

materials.title: B. Making a class audio programme
materials.text:
A class audio programme involves more than speaking into a microphone. Someone may enjoy writing, another presenting and another arranging the recordings. ____1____ A sensible division of work begins with these preferences rather than with one confident speaker doing everything.

Allow another attempt

Recording can make familiar words suddenly feel difficult. Before beginning, tell a nervous speaker, "____2____" Knowing that a mistake is not permanent can make the first attempt less stressful.

Keep recordings organised

After several attempts, files with almost identical names become hard to identify. ____3____ Then another group member can find the chosen version without listening to every file from the beginning.

Listen before sharing

Check the programme as a listener, not only as its makers. ____4____ A voice that sounds clear through large headphones may be difficult to understand on a small speaker if background music is too loud.

____5____

After the first programme, record one thing that worked and one thing to change. Perhaps the introduction was too long or the names of speakers were unclear. Keep those comments with the plan for the next programme, so each attempt can build on what the class has learned.
candidates: A. Give the selected version a clear topic and date in its name.
B. Play a short section on the kind of device your audience may use.
C. Only the loudest classmate should choose every role.
D. Use the experience next time
E. You can pause and record that sentence again.
F. Ask which parts each person would like to contribute to.
G. Once the first words are recorded, changing anything becomes impossible.
materials.instruction: Read the complete guide. Choose the best option for each gap. Two options are not needed. Keep the printed headings and quotation marks.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: F asks about the writing, presenting and arranging preferences listed before it. A is file naming, B playback, D a final heading and E a quoted reassurance. C ignores preferences; G wrongly makes recording irreversible.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: E is a reassuring second-person statement inside the printed quotation marks and links to mistakes not being permanent. A, B and F are task instructions, D a heading. C excludes others and G contradicts reassurance.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: A provides identifiable filenames and leads to finding the chosen version. B concerns listening devices, D reflection, E reassurance and F roles. C and G do not solve file confusion.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: B introduces playback on audience equipment, illustrated by headphones versus small speakers. A names files, D the later heading, E reassurance and F roles. C and G are unrelated restrictive claims.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 5.
questions.explanation: D heads the paragraph preserving lessons for the next programme. A, B, E and F are sentences serving other stages; C and G block the collaborative improvement described.
